periods.analysis: Port Everglades Shore Power Electrification opened the reporting arc at 7% complete and yellow, which is the right caution flag for a project that is still more paper-and-pathway than steel-and-copper. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is in-progress and sitting 15 days past plan, while Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults are not-started with 120 days to their due point and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs are not-started with 200 days to their due point. My watch-item is simple: the permit clock is already talking to us, and if we do not answer it with clean submittals and daily agency follow-up, the vault package will inherit the delay. The Harborview Harbor Energy team did complete the first utility-load walkdown from Substation E-4 to Berths 1, 2, and 3, which gives us a credible field basis rather than a conference-room estimate.
periods.recommendations: Hold yellow and put permitting on a daily closeout rhythm: assign one environmental lead to FDEP comments, one civil lead to Army Corps drawings, and publish a twice-weekly issue log until the 15-day slip is burned down. Keep Berth 1-3 vault procurement warm by advancing 60% design details for duct banks, switchgear pads, and cable routes even while the permit remains in-progress. Begin vessel-readiness outreach now with the three highest-call cruise operators so the MOUs do not become a late-stage commercial surprise.

periods.analysis: The initiative moved from 7% to 11% complete, up 4 percentage points quarter over quarter, but remains yellow because the controlling milestone has not changed. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is still in-progress and still 15 days past plan; Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults remain not-started with 120 days to their due point, and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs remain not-started with 200 days to their due point. The team used the quarter well by reconciling crane-clearance envelopes and underground conflict maps along the Berth 2 service road, but that is enabling work, not permit closure. I am encouraged by the discipline, not satisfied with the pace.
periods.recommendations: Keep the 4-point quarterly gain as the minimum burn rate, but do not let design coordination substitute for agency resolution. Convene a joint FDEP, Army Corps, Port Engineering, and utility review focused only on remaining permit objections, with decisions captured against drawing sheets SP-E101 through SP-E106. Prepare an early bid alternate for prefabricated vault sections at Berths 1-3 so procurement can move within ten business days once permitting clears.

periods.analysis: Progress advanced from 11% to 15% complete, another 4 percentage points quarter over quarter, and the project remains yellow rather than green because the same front-end constraint is still active. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is in-progress and 15 days past plan; Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults are not-started with 120 days to their due point, and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs are not-started with 200 days to their due point. Winter cruise volumes limited berth-access windows, so crews focused on night surveys, potholing near duct bank run DB-1A, and confirming the transformer delivery assumptions with the electrical vendor. That work reduces construction risk later, but it does not retire the watch-item: unresolved permit comments are now the critical path.
periods.recommendations: Maintain yellow and move to executive-level permit management, with Dana Okonkwo chairing a 30-minute Friday blocker review until the FDEP + Army Corps item is closed. Lock the berth-access calendar for shoulder-season windows before summer cargo and cruise schedules tighten again. Start drafting vessel-readiness MOU term sheets with shore-power connection standards, testing windows, and cost-sharing language so legal review can begin before the milestone formally starts.

periods.analysis: The project rose from 15% to 19% complete, up 4 percentage points quarter over quarter, preserving momentum but not yet changing the yellow posture. FDEP + Army Corps permitting remains in-progress and 15 days past plan, while Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults remain not-started with 120 days to their due point and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs remain not-started with 200 days to their due point. Field coordination improved this quarter: the port electrical crew and consultant designer completed a constructability walk for Vault V-1 and V-2 locations, including conflicts with stormwater inlet SD-23 and a fiber pull box serving gate cameras. The work is useful and practical, but I will not call the job healthy until permitting stops being a standing exception.
periods.recommendations: Convert the constructability findings into a permit-response package, not a separate design memo that sits on the shelf. Authorize limited pre-purchase review for long-lead switchgear and metering cabinets, with no notice to proceed until permit risk is formally accepted. Schedule cruise-line technical sessions by vessel class, starting with ships already wired for 11 kV shore connection, so the future MOU negotiations are about dates and testing rather than basic capability.

periods.analysis: Completion moved from 19% to 23%, again a 4 percentage point quarter-over-quarter gain, and the initiative is still yellow for the same reason: the first gate is not fully through the agencies. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is in-progress and 15 days past plan; Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults are not-started with 120 days to their due point, and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs are not-started with 200 days to their due point. The summer storm season gave us a useful stress test of temporary drainage assumptions around Berth 3, and the team adjusted the proposed vault rim elevations to account for nuisance tidal flooding. That is the kind of coastal discipline Harborview expects, but the watch-item remains permit closure before vault work starts to compress the schedule.
periods.recommendations: Keep the project yellow and require a storm-season addendum in the FDEP + Army Corps file so elevation changes are reviewed once, not reopened later. Direct Port Engineering to finalize the Berth 1-3 vault sequencing plan around cruise blackout dates and cargo gate operations. Use the updated tidal assumptions in cruise-line MOU drafts, including connection availability standards during minor flooding events and post-storm restart protocols.

periods.analysis: Port Everglades Shore Power Electrification increased from 23% to 27% complete, up 4 percentage points quarter over quarter, but yellow remains the honest rating. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is still in-progress and 15 days past plan; Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults are still not-started with 120 days to their due point, and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs are still not-started with 200 days to their due point. The team finished the 90% electrical one-line review for the Berth 1 feeder and validated that Substation E-4 can support phased energization with protective relay upgrades. Good engineering is showing up, but our public promise is shore power at the berth, not a better set of binders.
periods.recommendations: Treat the next quarter as the decision window: either close the FDEP + Army Corps permit path or bring forward a formal mitigation plan with schedule and cost exposure. Prepare the Berth 1 vault as the first construction package so crews can start in the least operationally disruptive footprint when released. Move the cruise-line MOU work from informal outreach to named negotiators, with one Harborview legal lead and one port commercial lead assigned to each carrier.

periods.analysis: The initiative advanced from 27% to 31% complete, maintaining the 4 percentage point quarter-over-quarter climb and staying yellow. FDEP + Army Corps permitting remains in-progress and 15 days past plan; Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults remain not-started with 120 days to their due point, and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs remain not-started with 200 days to their due point. The constructive news is that utility coordination has matured: Harborview Power accepted the preliminary relay settings for feeder HP-17, and the port team mapped a temporary construction laydown area outside the busiest passenger flow at Terminal C. Still, I am concerned about schedule elasticity; a project can move 4 points a quarter and still be late if the wrong gate stays open.
periods.recommendations: Keep yellow, but raise the watch-item to the Aviation & Seaport executive dashboard until permitting is no longer in-progress. Authorize a readiness drill for Berth 1 construction mobilization, including traffic control, laydown fencing, safety briefings, and utility outage communications. Push draft MOUs to the cruise lines with a 30-day response request, so vessel-readiness risk is visible before vault work begins.

periods.analysis: Completion moved from 31% to 35%, up 4 percentage points quarter over quarter, closing this eight-quarter run with steady progress but an unchanged yellow status. FDEP + Army Corps permitting is in-progress and 15 days past plan, while Berth 1-3 shore-power vaults remain not-started with 120 days to their due point and cruise-line vessel readiness MOUs remain not-started with 200 days to their due point. The arc is clear: the team has steadily de-risked engineering, utility interfaces, berth sequencing, and vessel outreach, but the formal permit gate has not yet cleared. In a fast-growing gateway port, disciplined caution is not pessimism; it is how we protect safety, cruise reliability, cargo flow, and Harborview’s sustainability commitments at the same time.
periods.recommendations: Continue the 4-point quarterly execution cadence, but require a permit recovery plan with named owners, agency response dates, and a no-later-than decision point for construction packaging. Advance Berth 1-3 vault bid documents to release-ready status, including alternates for prefabricated vaults and night-shift installation windows. Secure at least preliminary written alignment from the priority cruise operators on shore-power testing, plug standards, and vessel availability so the MOU milestone can start cleanly when authorized.
